Its HDMI input and IR blaster also let it connect to and control a cable box. For more on its performance, check out this PCMag review.

#3405. The 10 Greatest '90s TV Pilots, Ranked

Some TV shows take a while to get you invested, while others hook you right away. I was sold in the first five minutes of the Breaking Bad pilot episode, for example, while the new CBS legal drama Cupertino had me convinced to keep watching after episode one. But other shows are a slow burn. You might tell yourself you'll give three-to-four episodes before making a final decision about whether or not to continue.

The same goes for '90s shows. Some of them have you invested from the get-go. You just know they're going to be good, a sentiment that still holds true for new viewers who are checking them out today on streaming. There's something magical and engaging about how the core story is presented that draws you in. And in every case, it was worth it.

There was never a show's theme song, and hasn't been one since, that so perfectly describes what we're about to see. The rap, sung by Will Smith, who plays the title character in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, explains exactly what's about to happen so you can dive right into the story, even if you aren't watching from the first episode. As Will shows up at his aunt and uncle's house, it's clear he doesn't fit in. His street smarts and lack of refinement are on full display, juxtaposed with the rigidity of the others. You just know this is going to lead to comedy magic and one of the funniest shows of the 1990s.

One of the sweetest moments that suggests Will's antics, rebellious nature, and laissez-faire attitude are going to change things in this wealthy, uppity household is when he bonds with Ashley (Tatiana Ali), teaching her how to dance and rap. The scene when Will uses cutlery and drinkware to make music at a formal dinner with Uncle Phil's (James Avery) colleagues is absolute comedic perfection. You can't help but want to see more. And Phil's reprimand of Will and reveal of his own questionable past suggest there's going to be a lot of growth for all these characters.

The X-Files is one of the best sci-fi shows ever made, and right from the pilot, it was evident this show was going to be good. We meet FBI Special Agent Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson) and Special Agent Fox Mulder (David Duchovny), and the debate between science and logic and the unexplained begins.

It's the first time we see a glimmer of confusion with Scully when they unearth the body of a man but find a non-human corpse. The story itself of classmates who all died or went missing years ago is fascinating. It's indicative of the types of cases to come, and demonstrates the clever writing, wonderful effects, and compelling narratives of this show. The introduction of the Cigarette Smoking Man at the end is the perfect cliffhanger to leave you wanting more.

Twin Peaks sets the stage for its story right from the beginning: the body of a high school senior and homecoming queen has been discovered, and it's clear it was murder. Everyone in the small town is overcome by grief, unable to process what happened and who would do such a heinous thing.

Special Agent Dale Cooper (Kyle MacLachlan) is brought in, and so begins the murder mystery that you can't possibly stop watching until you find out what happened. Also intriguing about the pilot episode is the reveal that Laura Palmer (Sheryl Lee) was not exactly who everyone thought she was. She had a lot of secrets. Little nuggets of clues are dropped throughout the first episode, the perfect way to get fans hooked before they can even consider abandoning this show.

The idea behind ER was to present a raw and real look at the inner workings of a busy hospital emergency room, and there was no better way to do that than to show an entire 24-hour shift in a single hour. This is precisely what happened in the pilot episode, aptly called "24 Hours." Along with being introduced to the key figures, we're instantly acquainted with the frantic, emotional nature of the intense medical drama show. The chaos draws you in; the high-speed drama is like an action movie as you view the doctors and nurses as heroes, rooting for them to save lives in these cases that seem all too real.

But we also see the other side, including the pressures the staff feel in dealing with the trauma and balancing the demands of the job with their personal lives. A lot of it is viewed through the eyes of John Carter (Noah Wyle), a medical student who arrives for his first day on the job and is instantly overwhelmed. You feel like you're right there with him and can't wait to see what happens next.

A young woman kicking ass is pretty common in TV shows nowadays, but it wasn't as common back in the late '90s. So, the very premise of Buffy the Vampire Slayer was refreshing from the get-go. We get to see the set-up for the story in the pilot, with Buffy Summers (Sarah Michelle Gellar) moving to California and hoping to just be a regular teenager for once. But with Hellmouth under her new high school, a portal to demon dimensions, it means she'll have to reluctantly continue her work.

Buffy the Vampire Slayer's pilot episode perfectly balances telling a traditional coming-of-age story with a very non-traditional twist. Threats are instantly introduced, and you know there will be plenty of action to come that you won't want to miss out on.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Frasier came out of the gate with fans already knowing a lot about the title character, played by Kelsey Grammer. But it was surface-level, whatever he shared whenever he was enjoying a drink at the bar in Cheers. This sitcom, one of the most successful TV show spin-offs of all time, set out to dive deeper into his personal life. And this was well understood right from the beginning, reminding fans what made Dr. Frasier Crane so interesting in the first place.

Instantly, we got to meet Frasier's equally snooty and intellectual brother Niles (David Hyde Pierce), and it was evident that the dynamic between these brothers was going to show a different side to Frasier. There was also his producer Roz (Peri Gilpin) and his father's caretaker Daphne (Jane Leeves), who added a more traditional sitcom flavor to the comedy. It's perhaps Frasier's father, Martin (John Mahoney), however, who suggested we'd finally see how, even though Frasier had this air of superiority about him, the man who shaped him was so different from his sons that the comedy almost wrote itself.

When you see the title Everybody Loves Raymond, you aren't quite sure what to make of it. But the pilot episode of this sitcom made sure you understood right off the bat where everyone stands within Raymond Barone's (Ray Romano) orbit. He's a parent, but his wife Debra (Patricia Heaton) is clearly the disciplinarian. When Ray's family arrives, you quickly understand what the dynamic is. Ray is the "golden son" whose mother, Marie (Doris Roberts), dotes over while Robert (Brad Garrett) is often forgotten.

The idea of Debra being the hardworking housewife who takes on the brunt of the chores and child-rearing while dealing with constant passive-aggressive remarks from her judgemental mother-in-law is so relatable from the get-go. And the way the in-laws burst in suggests this isn't out of character for them, and the frustrations will intensify, as will the comedy.

The story in Friends, one of the most iconic sitcoms of all time, is about six young friends living in New York City. But it wasn't initially six. Rachel (Jennifer Aniston) joins as a newbie in the very first episode. While she's already an old friend of Monica's (Courteney Cox) and knows Ross (David Schwimmer) through her, she hasn't yet met the others. And boy, does she make an entrance.

In full Runaway Bride style, Rachel bursts into Central Perk, which we eventually learn is the group's favorite hangout, in full wedding dress attire. She's soaked and distraught, having just run out on her wedding. She knows she was making a mistake and needs a fresh start. Monica welcoming her old friend to the apartment with the words, "Welcome to the real world. It sucks! You're going to love it," perfectly captures what's to come for what turns out to be the next 10 seasons of TV comedic brilliance.

The idea of a news radio station being hip and cool is far from reality now in the day and age of streaming and podcasts. But the job was very different in the '90s, and it's captured wonderfully in the pilot of this episode. Dave Nelson (Dave Foley) is about to start his first day as news director of a fictional radio station. But he arrives at the wrong building, then has to rush to find the right one, reaching roadblocks at every turn. He finally makes it, frazzled while simultaneously trying to uphold his image as a professional who is prepared to lead.

It sets the tone for the show, especially when Dave is met with an equal level of chaos. He's, in a way, right at home even if his job is to bring a sense of calm and organization. He meets an eclectic group of employees, and we instantly get an idea of the dynamic and how each person will fit into the puzzle. The comedy is top-notch, confirming that this is a show that will make you laugh through every moment, every piece of dialogue.

The whole "walking and talking" down a long hallway filming technique was popularized by this show, and it was demonstrated in the very first episode of The West Wing. President Josiah Bartlet (Martin Sheen) sprains his ankle after hitting a tree on his bicycle, but that's just the tip of the iceberg of the drama unfolding. White House senior staff are called in to handle a variety of crises, and you just know this is simply day one of what will be a chaotic and frantic presidency.

From Deputy Chief of Staff Josh Lyman (Bradley Whitford), who lost his temper on a talk show and is facing potential termination, to Deputy Communications Director Sam Seaborn (Rob Lowe), who has been caught with a high-class escort, and tense situations with Cuban refugees crossing into Florida, it's apparently just another day at the office for Bartlet. You get the feeling that he will be a solid president, though. And a sense that the show, one of the best shows in network TV history, will tackle politics with a lens that is designed to make you think and debate, not judge.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3404. New leaks detail next year’s iPhone Pro redesign and iPhone Duo 2

Next year’s fall iPhone lineup is expected to include 20th anniversary redesigned Pro models and an iPhone Duo 2. Here’s what to expect per the latest leaks.

Rumors for next year’s flagship new iPhone models are ramping up. Earlier today, we got a release timing update on iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 and learned that Apple may have multiple iPhone 20 Pro designs in testing.

Now more details have arrived via Weibo leakers Digital Chat Station and Fixed Focus Digital, who focus on the highly-anticipated new iPhone Pro models and also the iPhone Duo 2.

Fixed Focus Digital says the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ will indeed return to a curved design, similar to the iPhone Air with more rounded edges. This echoes what the leaker shared earlier this week, but there’s one new tidbit: he says early prototypes include a titanium frame.

Apple used titanium for the iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, then abandoned it with the 17 Pro and 18 Pro. Titanium is used on the iPhone Air though. With next year’s 20th anniversary Pro models taking design cues from the Air, it sounds like titanium could return.

If faceID isn't coming to the Duo2 and there is no change to the screen size, then they should just keep selling the Duo1 next year and then come out with the Duo2 two years from now with faceID and a telephoto camera as tech gets smaller/better.

Leaker Digital Chat Station, in a reply to this post about iPhone Duo 2, adds that the 20 Pro series will be larger in size and have a bezel-free, quad-curved display.

Regarding the Duo 2, he says it will have the same 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer display as the first model. The side button with integrated Touch ID remains unchanged as well.

On the possibility of Face ID being added, he says it’s “questionable.” He suggests internal components might require too many changes, but doesn’t offer inside information.

Which new model are you more interested in: the iPhone 20 Pro or iPhone Duo 2? Let us know in the comments.

#3401. You Can Save up to $160 on Headphones From Bose, Sony, and Apple With These Early Black Friday Deals

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts to wireless headphones, with savings of up to $160 across models from Sony, Bose, Apple, Nothing, and other brands. Several of the headphones on sale are relatively new, including Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro and Bose's second-generation QuietComfort Headphones, both of which launched this fall. Better yet, most of the deals below have dropped to their lowest prices yet on Amazon.

There's a good mix to choose from, too, whether you're looking for premium noise-canceling headphones for flights and commutes, a pair with enough battery life to get you through a week of listening, or something inexpensive for everyday use, with prices starting under $50. You can also check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage for more editor-vetted tech deals as the sale continues.

The Nothing Headphone (a) is down to a record-low $109 from $199, making it a solid option for everyday listening, especially for Android users who can take advantage of LDAC for higher-quality wireless audio. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Spending another $60 gets you the Nothing Headphone (1), now $169 from $299, which is also a record low. It offers a more premium listening experience with active noise cancellation, automatic playback pausing when you take the headphones off, and the option to listen through either USB-C or a 3.5mm cable, making it a well-rounded choice for everyday use. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Nothing's newest and most expensive over-ears, the Headphone (1) Pro, are already $80 off at $319, only a couple of months after launching at $399. This is the pair to get for sound quality, since Nothing moved to a three-driver setup in each earcup, and the result is a fuller, more detailed sound than either the Headphone (1) or Headphone (a). For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Sony's flagship WH-1000XM6 headphones are down to $378 from $459.99, their lowest price yet. Noise cancellation is still the main reason to buy them, and they remain among the best options for blocking out engine rumble on a flight, traffic during a commute, or chatter in a busy office. For more on these over-ears, you can check out our in-depth review.

Sony's WH-CH730N brings noise cancellation down to a much more approachable price, and at $98, down from $179.99, it's the lowest it's been on Amazon. This 2026 update to Sony's budget noise-canceling line now folds up for travel, which the previous model couldn't do, and battery life has jumped to up to 50 hours with noise cancellation on.

Sony's WH-CH530 is the most affordable pair in this roundup at $38, down from $69.99—that's also the lowest it's been since its release this fall. These are simple on-ear headphones without noise cancellation, but they sound better than you'd expect at this price, and the battery lasts up to 55 hours, so a full week of commuting or classes shouldn't be a problem.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, their lowest price yet. That's a substantial discount for a pair that delivers on two of Bose's biggest strengths: comfort and noise cancellation. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

Bose's flagship QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen) are down to $339 from $449, saving you $110. Their noise cancellation is among the best you'll find in consumer headphones, making them particularly appealing for frequent flyers or anyone who spends a lot of time in noisy environments. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

The 2026 JBL Tune 680NC are down to $49.95 from $109.95, their lowest price to date. That's a pretty good deal for anyone looking for affordable noise-canceling headphones, especially since you get adaptive noise cancellation that adjusts to your surroundings and up to 50 hours of battery life with it enabled.

For the same price, JBL's Tune 730BT trades noise cancellation for a larger over-ear fit and even longer battery life, rated at up to 76 hours. At $49.95, down from $89.95, it's at its lowest price on Amazon, and a sensible choice for anyone who mostly listens at home, at a desk, or on quieter commutes where noise cancellation isn't essential.

The JBL Live 780NC are down to $129.95 from $249.95, making them considerably more appealing than at their original price. Battery life is a major advantage here, with JBL estimating up to 50 hours with noise cancellation enabled and 80 hours without, so frequent charging shouldn't be a concern. They also support LDAC for higher-quality Bluetooth audio with compatible devices. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

Apple’s AirPods Max 2 are down to $449 from $549, saving you $100 on the second-generation over-ears that Apple released earlier this year. While the design hasn’t changed much from the original, the upgrade to Apple’s H2 chip brings improved noise cancellation, while its sound remains among the best you'll find in wireless headphones. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

Soundcore's Q20i headphones are down to $42.69 from $69.99, making them one of the more affordable options for anyone looking for noise-canceling over-ears from a recognizable brand. They're particularly worth considering for students, occasional travelers, or anyone who wants a budget-friendly backup pair.

The Beats Solo 4 are down to $129.95 from $199.95, saving you $70. While these lightweight on-ear headphones don't have active noise cancellation, they offer plenty of flexibility for everyday listening, whether you're using an iPhone or an Android phone, with quick pairing on both platforms, notes this PCMag review.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones have the largest dollar discount in this roundup, dropping $160 from $359 to $199.

That depends on how much you want to spend and where you'll use them. The Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) are worth considering for frequent travelers who prioritize noise cancellation, while the regular Bose QuietComfort Headphones at $199 offer a more affordable premium option. #3400. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important issues and leaves out key context. The company says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

#3396. Instagram finally lets users edit Stories after publishing, but there’s a catch

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that users will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:

Today’s update is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting users manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

#3393. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

#3390. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3383. Hunger Games Director Officially Teases the Franchise’s Future Beyond ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’

Editor's note: The following contains spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

After the first movie, director Francis Lawrence took the reins of the Hunger Games franchise with 2013’s Catching Fire. He collaborated with author Suzanne Collins, established a family with the cast and crew, led by Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen, and returned for each subsequent film as Collins continued to find inspiration through the years to pick up the pen again — once for The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, and again with the upcoming follow-up prequel, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

This most recent addition, Lawrence tells Collider’s Steve Weintraub, was a big surprise. The story of young Haymitch Abernathy, played by relative newcomer Joseph Zada, was at the top of book fans’ lists, but so soon after President Snow’s (Tom Blyth) prequel was an unexpected treat. “We're just as surprised as anybody else when the book's announced,” Lawrence admits, though he does get official early access. In Sunrise, Lawrence and the team were tasked with finding the perfect casting for the 50th Hunger Games, from the younger versions of known characters like President Snow (Ralph Fiennes), Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning), and Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), to brand-new faces like the fiery Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace), Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close), and District 12’s Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang).

During a recent interview with Lawrence, the filmmaker discusses the making of the movie, including the major book scene that was cut from the film, the casting process, bringing back the OG trio — Lawrence, Woody Harrelson, and Josh Hutcherson — and whether we’ll be getting more Hunger Games in the future. Check out the full interview below for more on Sunrise on the Reaping, plus the Oscar-winning films Lawrence passed on, his most insane story from his time directing music videos with Britney Spears, Justin Timberlake, Lada Gaga, and more, and why the recent DC Studios shakeup may spell success for Constantine 2.

COLLIDER: If I were to watch the first assembly cut of the film, what would be the biggest difference between that version and the movie audiences are about to see?

FRANCIS LAWRENCE: The bulk of the movie is very similar. I'd say a lot of it is the trimming of the fat. There are a few sequences that got cut. There’s a sequence right before the interviews where Drusilla’s character does some coaching of Haymitch and Lou Lou and Wyatt and Maysilee in the green room before they go out on stage, and we cut that sequence. So that was maybe 10 minutes, but that was an area that I felt needed to be compressed anyway. We were also trying to tie Effie's character in a little more specifically, so that was one big cut.

And then there was another chunk in the arena that we shot that was in for a while that's probably another 10-minute piece. That’s after that sequence where the bugs all stick onto their skin, and then they wash off in the rain. So when they're sitting there in the rain, they hear some people start screaming, and they hear some cannons, and they go investigate to search some packs, and they get ambushed and get chased by a couple of other tributes and end up coming face to face with some Gamemakers that are actually in the arena trying to make some repairs.

It's a sequence that I think a lot of fans are probably going to be surprised that got omitted, but it existed in the book as part of the theme of implicit submission. Once we sort of built the movie, and we watched it, really, Nina [Jacobson] and I, and then Suzanne [Collins] also finally agreed, we really felt like at this point in the movie, Haymitch was no longer submitting, so we did not need to have a sequence about him still submitting and getting into an argument with Maysilee about submitting. We felt like he was far, far beyond that, and having been down to Sub A and attempting that first explosion and doing everything he's doing, so we ended up lifting that sequence.

With a sequence like that, even though it takes place further in the movie, was there ever a debate about moving the sequence forward?

LAWRENCE: No, because it wouldn't work. He wouldn't have reunited with Maysilee by that time. If we moved it up ahead, then he would be with her, then not with her. The timeline wouldn't work.

The movie's two hours and 38 minutes. How much is going on behind the scenes from the studio perspective, being like, “Hey, the most you can release is 2.38?” How much is there to debate behind the scenes in terms of knowing we don't want to release a three-hour movie, or is there the option of, down the road, you could release an extended cut which has all these scenes in it?

LAWRENCE: First of all, I've never wanted to release an extended cut. I've never found myself in this situation. I'm happy to release deleted scenes for fans that want to see scenes that were shot, and they can see them out of context. But I've never made a movie where I felt like somebody forced me to cut a chunk of the movie out for time, and I really believed that needed to be in there. So, I've never been in that situation before.

The truth is, runtime for me is much more about feel than it is about actual length. The only thing that annoys me now about people watching movies is people tend to click up on a thumbnail, and you see a runtime, which may make them decide whether or not they want to watch it — and a Rotten Tomatoes score. So I wish they would just know what the movie's about and go and watch it. So, runtime for me is really just about the fact that it's like a little tag next to the name of the movie. Whether you're watching it at a theater, at home, on an airplane, or whatever, it's really about feel.

Luckily, every studio that I've worked with so far has been about if the movie plays and people feel like it's moving and people aren't getting bored, and it's not feeling slow and sluggish, the time doesn't matter. I feel like there's a tipping point. Somebody told me this once, and I don't know if it's still true, because the way exhibitors work, things are always changing, but I think there is a tipping point around the three-hour mark where you actually truly start to lose shows in a day. So it can actually sort of affect box office over a certain point. But I believe if you're somewhere under three, and I don't have the exact science, you're not losing showings in a day, and all that kind of stuff. So, if a movie's working and moving and keeping people engaged, it doesn't bother me.

The other thing that drives me a little crazy about time is the movie is actually under two and a half hours. The problem is, credits on a movie of this size are, with main-on-ends and end credits, 10 or 11 minutes long. So, the actual movie is under two and a half, but because of the credits, it gets stuck on, and then it looks like it's a two-hour, 40-minute movie to people.

I wish more people understood that for some movies, an hour and 50 minutes is the perfect length, but when you are dealing with a movie like Hunger Games, where you are having all these new characters, and you want to meet these characters and feel for them, you need time to have scenes where you're talking that don't have action, that in a two-hour movie or an hour and 50-minute movie, you're not going to have those scenes. It's only because you're closer to 2.5 hours that you can put in 30 minutes’ worth of people talking.

LAWRENCE: Yes. But again, it's about the dynamics of the movie, too. Things have to be happening. But if things are happening and you have dynamic peaks as you're going throughout, when those things happen, it buys you a little time. So there's something sort of instinctual, I believe, about the building of a movie, of finding those moments where you can create those dynamic pops that buy you a little time to sit with characters for a minute.

Then you need another one of those dynamic hits — and that could be a story turn, it could be an action sequence, it could be somebody dies. I mean, who knows what those things are, but I think you need those things. But then once you have it, then you have a little room for quiet.

When you made the last Hunger Games movie, you thought that was probably it. You were probably thinking, “This is the end of my Hunger Games life,” or did you know when you were filming that she was writing this book?

LAWRENCE: No. She never tells us if she's writing anything. She's sort of superstitious about it. Not sure if that's the right word, but she definitely does not tell us about it until she feels like she has a somewhat finished manuscript.

This was probably the earliest that she ever showed us one of her books, but it was still a surprise. So when she called, and I saw she was calling my cell phone, I was shocked because I was not expecting that to happen, and especially that soon. Then also, when she tells me she has a book, she doesn't tell us what it is, so we basically have to go to her agent's house and go sit in the backyard, and there's a manuscript, and you open it up, and we're just as surprised as anybody else when the book's announced.

So this could be the last time with Hunger Games.

LAWRENCE: It could. I hope not. I like working with Suzanne and Nina and everybody. I love it, but it certainly could be the last one.

You've spent such a chapter of your life making these films. Do you mentally let go? What is it like for you knowing that this could be the end of this part, or that it still could continue if she decides to write another book?

LAWRENCE: I don't know if I mentally let go. I feel like I'm in a zone. When we finished The Mockingjays, that original batch, because it was like back to back to back to back, I was like, “Okay, I need a break from this.” I know Suzanne needed a break from this. And then everybody kind of went off and did different things. Nina did different things; I did; Suzanne tried some different things.

Then we got surprised because she got inspired and she wrote the last one. Then it was like, okay, great. We sort of cleansed our palettes in a way, and we got to come back. Then, when we were making that one, we didn't know if that was just going to be a one-off and whether or not she was going to be inspired again. So, I think I've sort of just resigned myself to the idea of, like, I sit back and enjoy the suspense of whether or not she's going to write something again and whether or not I'm going to see her name pop up on my phone to tell me whether she's just calling to say hi or calling to tell me that there's a new manuscript to read.

So, something to look forward to. But I've definitely stopped guessing or stopped trying to come up with ideas of what other movies could be and all of that, since it always has to come from her.

I know a lot of directors and some of them have told me that they really like to collect stuff from their movies. Guillermo [del Toro] likes to take home everything. With all these Hunger Games movies and other films you've worked on, how much do you like taking home things from the films, and how much are you like, “I don't care?”

LAWRENCE: I don't really care too much. I mean, Keanu gave me the holy shotgun from Constantine that I can see right up there on my shelf. That was a very cool gift. So that's probably one of the cooler things I have.

I have a couple of arrows from the original Hunger Games movies, the original series, because the arrows change throughout the series, based on where she is, if she's in an arena, if she's at home, or if she's in The Mockingjay — exploding tips and things like that. So, I have some arrows.

But yeah, I don't have too many things. I have some ballet shoes that Jen [Lawrence]’s ballet double gave me from Red Sparrow. So I have a couple things. But Guillermo basically has, like, a museum.

I would be taking costumes and other things, but that's just who I am.

LAWRENCE: Some of the actors do that. There are different people that do those kinds of things, like steal costumes or little pieces or trinkets and props and things like that.

I mean, I also have, sometimes, weird things, like I'm looking at a clock that I have that was in Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. The art department on these last two movies is so good, and the props department is so good. I remember it was in Coryo Snow's apartment, where he lived. There was just this very, very cool clock, and I talked to one of the prop designers who was on set, who I'm friends with, and asked about the clock, and then she gifted it to me. So I've got that. But that, honestly, was just because I thought it was a cool clock.

I definitely have to talk about bringing back Jen, Josh [Hutcherson], and Woody [Harrelson]. Talk a little bit about getting them to come back. Was it one of these things where they jumped at the chance to reprise their roles for a day? How did that come together?

LAWRENCE: Basically the plan was we all hoped we would be able to figure out an epilogue that would include them because they're included in the book. Their presence is at the end of the book, so I think we knew fans would be speculating. There's an element to having them at the end of this story that is cathartic, which I thought was important, but we were never sure we were going to be able to make it happen — and this was before we asked them — just because you never know what people's schedules are going to be like and whether or not you can count on certain things.

So, we kind of tasked ourselves with working on an adaptation that we felt could work without them. That was the thing. And then we would come up with something with them that, like, if we got them and they wanted to do it, we could make everything work, awesome, but if not, we felt confident that we could finish this movie in a way that would still feel fulfilling and satisfying and cathartic, especially after the kind of story we've just gone through.

Basically, we started talking about when to approach them, and this was before the book was even announced. So we decided, because I will say, out of love, two of the three of those people are slightly unfiltered people, and so we couldn't let them know necessarily too soon because you don't want anything to accidentally slip before the book is even announced. So I basically texted the three of them that I wanted to chat with them about something to do with The Hunger Games the day before the book came out, and they all called me back instantly.

I talked to Jen first, and I think she squealed and was super, super excited and wanted to jump in, for sure. Woody was down. Josh was down. Josh was funny, too, because I think he thought I was calling like something was wrong, like I was going to give him some sort of bad news about his character, or something. I’m like, “No, we actually want you guys to come back.” So they all wanted to do it. Then it really just became about, “Stay quiet for the next day until the book's announced, and then obviously don't say anything about being in the movie,” which they kept quiet for a while. [Laughs]

Then it was really just about figuring out schedules because they all wanted to come back, and they all love each other, and it's the same crew. Luckily, this is a franchise that people aren't embarrassed by. So it's not like this is a group of people that made these movies and they're happy to have been done with them, and they're out of their lives forever. So they were, I think, very happy to come back for half a day of shooting.

Where did you actually shoot their stuff and how long did it take?

LAWRENCE: They came to Germany. Basically, we started this movie in Spain, where we did the Games. So we shot out there for about six weeks, I'd say. Yeah, five or six weeks. Something like that. And then we moved to the west of Germany, to the Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg area, and Duisburg is where our District 12 is. That's where we do the Reaping and all the basic District 12 stuff at the beginning and the end of the movie. So we got them to come out and stay with us in Düsseldorf and do a half-day shoot at our Duisburg location at Landgraf Park, where the actual Reaping square is. But yeah, they were out in Germany with us.

What was it like right before the first take with the three of them? What's that energy like figuring out how you wanted to shoot them, what it was going to look like? I would imagine that's a really cool, special energy having the three of them back on the set of a Hunger Games movie.

LAWRENCE: It was cool. I have to say, the best thing, though, was actually two days before that. It was when they showed up in Germany. I remember I was coming back from a day — I don't remember where it was; it was like a forest or something — and I had rain gear on, and my shoes were muddy, and all this, and Jen texted me and said, “Me and Josh are in the bar. We're here. We're in the bar having a beer. Let us know when you're back.” And I said, “Oh, I'm almost back. I'm just going to take a shower.” Then I said, you know what? Fuck it. I don't need to take a shower, and I just walked into the bar in my rain gear and saw them.

Then Nina came in, and then Woody and his wife came in, and then our cinematographer came in, and the camera operator came in, and the still photographer came in, and it was that group of people that ended up being, I don't know, 30 of us or something, that the bulk of had been making these movies since 2012. Some of them, Nina and even the still photographer, have been there since the first one. So, that was the special time, was to know that, like, oh, the whole gang is back together and we're here for this, to make one of these again.

Then some of the new cast came in, like Joe [Zada] came in and I think Whitney [Peak] was around. I don't remember if McKenna [Grace] came in that evening or not, but a bunch of the new cast came in and met everybody, too, and that was really nice. But that was the night before they had their fittings and hair, makeup, wardrobe tests, and that kind of stuff.

Then we shot the day after that, and shooting's fun, too, but I think it was the reunion for the purpose of making this and being in Germany and everything together. That was really fun.

It's a great ending. It's so good, and it ties it all together. But I’m curious, have you revealed what the ending would have been had they not done it?

LAWRENCE: Yeah, I think it would have been baby Katniss. I think it would have been knowing that Katniss was born. So, it would have been that idea where he sees his friends, who he's isolated himself from, and they now have a baby, and he overhears and sees and makes eye contact with the baby Katniss for the first time.

A lot of people don't realize the importance of the casting director. You're getting ready to make this — how much are you in your head thinking about what actors you want? Can you talk a little bit about collaborating with your casting director? You have a big, big cast to fill, and you put together this murderer's row of great actors, so talk a little bit about what that dynamic is like.

LAWRENCE: Well, Deb [Zane], who's done all these movies, and her associate Dylan [Jury], they're great people. They're great at casting. They have great taste, great ideas. So, I think one of the things that happens is we start to talk about the characters and where they are in their lives and all of that. And then, you put lists together. These lists are for the people that you know are going to be established actors, right? It's going to be for the Caesars, the Snows, the Effies, all of that kind of stuff.

So basically, just based on that, I made my first choices of, yeah, Ralph [Fiennes], I would love to work with Ralph, and Ralph could be Snow. He'd be perfect. And luckily he wanted to do it. Jesse [Plemons] was actually the first person we cast. I don't even think I looked at a list for him. I think I just knew I wanted Jesse, and so we got him. Luckily, he wanted to do it. He read the book. We didn't even have a script yet for him, but we got him.

Elle [Fanning] I knew because I did a commercial with her when she was 19, and I just think she's great. I thought she'd be a perfect Effie, so we went after her. Kieran [Culkin] I also thought, and I think nobody, including me, thought he would ever say yes, and it took a minute to get him on a Zoom with me. But once we did, we kind of locked in, and he said yes. Glenn [Close] actually approached us and said she was interested in becoming a part of the franchise and wanted to take part in it. I was a huge fan from The World According to Garp and Dangerous Liaisons and Fatal Attraction, and so, of course, yes.

There are definitely discussions, but I will say with that group, it felt like those choices were easy, in a weird way, and then luckily they all said yes. So, they definitely do some chasing down and chatting to people to make the Zooms happen and figure out schedules and all that kind of stuff.

I think where they really shine is the world of all the actors, like the people that we are unfamiliar with, because these movies are basically built on young, up-and-coming actors, and then established veteran actors. It's when they go and they find people like Joe Zada.

Deb is the one who really just said, “You guys have to sit down with this kid.” And so we sat down with him, and he had made this improv tape because that was what we did before we had pages, because the book wasn't out yet. We basically had people create their own version of scenes of Young Haymitch, just to sort of see the lay of the land of, like, who's out there at that age? Who's interesting? Who's not? Who's possibly right, who's possibly wrong? So for her to put Joe in front of us and have us work with him, and for her to put Whitney in front of us and have us work with her.

She sent pages to McKenna. I was familiar with McKenna’s stuff. I've had a friend do a movie with her before. But again, just to have Deb send her the stuff and for her to read for the role, and Maya [Hawke], too. Even to put Maya in front of us, and Iris [Apatow] in front of us, I think that's, for me, where they really shine because that's where their knowledge of the new up-and-coming, haven't-really-done-anything-yet people they think can pop, the people that have talent but also have charisma, that have that extra sort of effervescence to them that’s so kind of magical, I think that's where they really shine.

If people could see a list of all the movies you've been offered but didn't do, what's the one that people would be most shocked to see?

LAWRENCE: I'm not sure offered is the right term, like I was offered and turned down. But some things that I was actually on and developed for a while, one of them is The Revenant. I was on The Revenant for a while and tried to develop that and couldn't quite crack it, and Alejandro [G. Iñárritu] did. After I was off of it, he figured that one out and did a fantastic job.

I developed a version of The Odyssey years ago, which is also a tricky one. I'm trying to think of what else is out there.

LAWRENCE: Yeah. Unbroken. That was another one that I don't think got cracked, actually, and we hadn’t figured it out yet. That's the story about Louis Zamperini in World War II.

Oh, yeah. Angelina Jolie ended up doing it.

LAWRENCE: Angelina Jolie ended up doing it, yes. But that was my project, and I met with Louis many, many times before he passed away. Then I got Catching Fire, actually. Originally, I was going to keep it and keep working on it because I didn't think we had figured it out yet, and then I got the Mockingjay sequel, so I knew I was going to be gone for a while, and I wanted somebody to make the movie before Louis died, so I let it go.

But yeah, The Revenant I let go because I couldn't crack it, as much as I loved that story. The Odyssey, the same thing. I couldn't really crack the kind of episodic nature of it. And also, quite honestly, cracking the real Odysseus, the guy with pride and hubris. He's a tricky character.

Listen, I ask you this every time or anytime I'm talking to Keanu [Reeves] or Akiva [Goldsman]: Do you think Constantine 2 will actually happen, and with the new owners, do you think it's more of a possibility now?

LAWRENCE: Well, I'll tell you this. Not that I want anybody to lose their jobs, so this is not like a schadenfreude kind of thing, but I will say that we've been trying to make Constantine 2 for 20-something years, and we have an idea, and we have a script, and we've been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it. So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday's news that maybe now there will be another opportunity.

But again, we've been trying to make this for 20-something years, and there's always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it's not me, it's not Keanu, it's not Akiva. J.J. [Abrams] is on it, as well. We all want to do it. So, it's really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever's running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, “Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of Constantine.”

Personally, I don't even care if somebody has a plan for some sort of shared universe and they want to do another version of Constantine, if they just let us do the sequel to our version, they can coexist. So, I have renewed hope as of yesterday that there might be some possibility for forward movement there.

The script that you guys have, or the story you guys are happy with, I'm assuming it's rated R?

LAWRENCE: Yes. So, part of the idea from the very beginning was because we followed all the rules to make a PG-13 movie, and we got hit with an R. They told us, “You can't do anything about it. It's going to be an R no matter what.” We tried to fight them on it and they said, “Nope. It's an R.” But really, it's an R-rated PG-13 movie, which pisses me off.

And so we all kind of came back and said, “Okay, when we do this next time, we're making the hard-R version of Constantine.” So when we do it, it's going to be the hard-R version of Constantine.

I'm just going to be honest, I don't see a Constantine sequel as being a four-quadrant movie. This is being made for fans and a select part of the audience. So how much when you guys were figuring out the sequel were you thinking, “We're not going to get $150 million to make this?”

LAWRENCE: We were thinking that a lot. That's always been the plan, and we keep talking about it now. We have to be responsible. We want to make it. This is not the kind of movie that I would charge full freight, and Keanu could charge full freight. It's something we have to do because we love and want to take a gamble on it, and do it responsibly. And so we've been thinking about that same idea for 20 years, that we're not going to do it for $100 million. We have to be scrappy about it.

Watch Collider's first ever "Producers on Producing" panel.

Early in your career, you directed a ton of music videos. You worked with Britney Spears, Lady Gaga, J.Lo, a ton of people. Now that it's been such a long period of time, what's the craziest thing you witnessed on a music video set that you were like, “I can't believe I'm looking at this?”

LAWRENCE: I don't want to throw the artist under the bus, but there was an artist that was very problematic, just in terms of shooting. It's like the person was sort of, personally, very cool, and you could have nice conversations, but there were a lot of things going on in the shooting. It was a three-day shoot, and both the first and second day got sort of derailed by this person, and so the bulk of what we needed to do needed to get shot on the third day, which turned it into the longest shoot day I've ever had, which was 26 hours, which you would never be allowed to do anymore. This was 2001 or something — which is probably hinting too much about who this could possibly be.

But yeah, we did a 26-hour day, and it was probably 9:00 in the morning, hour 26, and we were doing the last shot, and it was a person getting dropped into water on these wires, and, yeah, they demanded to eat something between takes. I just needed one more take, and we could wrap, and they sort of demanded to eat, and sat there hanging on the edge of the tank, eating banana chips for 20 minutes, with the whole crew staring daggers at this person. I think that was probably the craziest thing.

I mean, I didn't see any wild drug use or any weird tantrums or anything like that. It was just how sort of thoughtless this person was about what this crew had just been through for three days, and then specifically this last 26-hour day. It was wild.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters now.

#3380. 5-Year-Old Boy Shot In The Head After Gun Was Left Unsecured in His Family's Home

A 5-year-old boy was critically injured after being shot in the head -- and police say it’s all because a gun was apparently left unsecured in his family’s Michigan home.

Detroit Police Department Deputy Chief, Sonia Russell, told reporters that the Friday evening shooting occurred while the boy was horsing around downstairs with 2 other kids -- ages 2 and 4. Russell said the boy’s mom and another relative were upstairs and they heard a gunshot before rushing downstairs.

According to media reports, police believe that one of the kids got their hands on an unsecured firearm, which suddenly discharged -- and a bullet struck the 5-year-old in his head, causing him to fall face first to the floor.

Russell said the boy was still alive, but in critical condition at a local hospital, adding that his mom was "hysterical." The two other kids do not have reported injuries.

The deputy chief also said the firearm was not recovered -- and officers are now trying to locate the gun.

According to Fox 2, a suspect is now in custody ... but no information is available yet on their identity.

Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison urged adults to secure their firearms, saying that leaving a gun unsecured is negligent, especially when it leads to a child being harmed. Bettison warned that "someone's going to jail" when that happens.

Siri Modular, the new Apple Watch face in watchOS 27, is gaining new style options. watchOS 27.3, currently in beta, adds two more style options to the existing set. This gives users five options for adjusting what type of information appears on Siri Modular.

Siri Modular originally shipped with three style options. Each supports a small line complication above the time.

Additionally, the original three styles include these options:

In watchOS 27.3, Apple introduces two new Siri features that work with Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

First, there’s Siri Recap which uses the Apple Watch to turn audio into high-level text summaries. Second, there’s Live Rewind which lets you view a transcript of the last 15 seconds of spoken word.

The two new Siri Modular Apple Watch face styles help surface three things: invoking Siri, viewing conversations with Siri, and viewing Siri Recaps on the Apple Watch.

The new styles include a pill-shaped module that includes icon shortcuts that go directly to Siri conversations, invoke Siri AI, or go directly to Siri Recaps in the Siri app.

One style features a large digital clock with the new three-button Siri module. Another includes a compact digital clock with a Smart Stack tile and the new three-button Siri module.

This brings the style options to five. If you use the three circular complications configuration, you can also assign a Siri icon that invokes Siri AI.

watchOS 27.3 is currently in beta and expected to be released officially in December.

#3374. The Best Tech Deals From Costco's Early Black Friday Sale

Sam's Club, Walmart, Amazon, and other retailers have been churning out early Black Friday deals since last week, so if you haven't been paying attention, you've already missed out on some good deals. But all hope is not lost: Costco recently started its own early sale, so you're still in time to find something you want at a low price. Below, I've rounded up my favorite tech deals from their sale—but keep in mind you'll need a membership to take advantage of these deals.

A powerful monitor with high-end specs can make gaming more immersive and greatly reduce input lag, which is helpful for any serious gamer looking for an edge over their opponents. The Samsung Odyssey G9 is a 49-inch gaming monitor with some impressive specs, including a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1 ms response time. It's available for $699.99 (originally $899.99), $200 off and the lowest price it has reached this year.

If you're looking for a more premium (and far more massive) gaming monitor, the 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,449.99 ($2,499.99 at launch). This monitor came out in 2023, earning an "excellent" review from PCMag for its impressive 7,680 x 2,160 4K resolution, its great color range and accuracy, a 240Hz refresh rate, 1,000 nits of brightness, and its overall design. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful graphics card. But if you have the right setup, this thing really delivers.

The 15.3-inch Lenovo Legion is a powerful gaming laptop with premium specs, and with the current $600 discount, it's down to $1999.99 (originally $2,599.99). It has a powerful AMD Ryzen AI 9 processor, 32 GB of RAM, a GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, and 1TB of SSD. PCMag gave the more affordable 5i version an excellent review for its price and performance, so if you have the cash for it, this one is even better.

A soundbar is a great way to improve a home entertainment system without spending too much money. This 5.1 TCL Q6CH setup is currently $199.99 (originally $299.99), including a soundbar and subwoofer. This soundbar came out in 2024 and supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X for that 3D sound, as well as AI Sonic, a tool that tunes your sound settings based on the setup of your room.

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up from their previous generation. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds deliver a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation: They're $179 at Costco (originally $249) in an early Black Friday deal.

The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,249 (originally $1,499), the lowest price since Apple hiked prices this past summer. The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Air, the M5 base model has double the storage, and the powerful M5 chip makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, and it includes a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

The 15.6-inch Acer Aspire Go is a great value at its current $499.99 price (originally $699.99). The display is a touchscreen; it sports an AMD Ryzen 5 processor and it has 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. These aren't specs you normally find at this price, making it a great laptop for anyone looking to stretch their money as far as possible while getting a workhorse of a laptop.

I'm a fan of TCL TVs, and currently own the "non-pro" version of this TV. The 65-inch QM6K Pro is $599.99 (originally $999.99) and has the same internal hardware and Mini-LED panel as the regular QM6K, but it adds a CrystGlow anti-reflective coating that makes it more viewable in well-lit rooms and helps maintain a high picture contrast. The 144 Hz native refresh rate makes gaming smooth, and support for Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG means you're well positioned to get the best sound quality when streaming movies or shows.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.
